UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                   )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )                     Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                   )

    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE LIMITED ANSWER, AND LIMITED ANSWER OF
            SOUTHERN MARYLAND ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

I. Introduction and Summary

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission ("Commission"), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213, Southern Maryland

Electric Cooperative, Inc. ("SMECO") respectfully moves for leave to file this limited answer

(“Limited Answer”) and answer to the September 23, 2026 Answer of PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. ("PJM") filed in the above-captioned docket on September 23, 2026 ("PJM Answer").

        On September 3, 2026, SMECO filed Comments and Limited Protest ("SMECO Limited

Protest")1 regarding PJM's August 13, 2026 proposal to establish Interim Resource Adequacy

Service ("IRAS") and a Large Load Registry ("IRAS Filing"). SMECO's Limited Protest raised

three discrete issues affecting Electric Distributors:

     1. The real-time Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action mechanism does not confirm
        that the New Large Load underlying an Electric Distributor's assigned obligation is actually
        energized, risking curtailment of the Electric Distributor's core native load.2
     2. The billing indemnification provision in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section
        X(b)(iii) shifts compensation default risk to Electric Distributors, including for payments
        owed by unaffiliated entities.3
     3. The Large Load Registry rests on Manual provisions not yet developed, leaves unclear the
        scope of Electric Distributor liability for third-party data, and identifies no cost-recovery
        mechanism (Section IV.D). 4

 The PJM Answer does not respond to any of SMECO's issues. PJM states that its "silence on any

argument should not be deemed as acceptance of the arguments raised."5 But silence also supplies

no record basis on which the Commission can resolve these issues. As the filing utility under

section 205 of the Federal Power Act ("FPA"), PJM bears the burden of demonstrating that its

proposal is just and reasonable.6 The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities ("NJBPU"), moreover,

has filed an answer supporting SMECO's position on the first of these issues.7

        SMECO therefore respectfully requests that, in acting on the IRAS Filing, the Commission

direct PJM to make the clarifications and revisions described below, either on compliance or before

the relevant provisions take effect.


II. Motion for Leave to Answer

        Although Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits answers to protests or answers absent

Commission authorization, the Commission accepts otherwise-prohibited answers when they

provide information that assists its decision-making,8 and clarify the record.9 Good cause exists

here to justify the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this Limited Answer. This

Limited Answer raises no new issues and is narrow. It identifies for the Commission issues in

SMECO's Limited Protest that remain unaddressed on the record. PJM has asked the Commission

III. Answer

A. PJM Did Not Respond to SMECO's Showing That an IRAS Action Could Require
Curtailment of Core Native Load.

         SMECO showed that, under the Affidavit of Christopher Pilong, an Interim Resource

Adequacy Service Action directs an Electric Distributor to reduce load up to its full pre-Delivery

Year IRAS obligation. That quantity is fixed before the Delivery Year and is not tied to whether

the underlying New Large Load is energized and taking service. No IRAS Alert need precede an

Action.10 Eligible New Large Loads are, by definition, loads that have not brought their own

capacity, and are disproportionately likely to still be under construction or commissioning.11 If

such a load is not yet drawing power when an Action issues, the Electric Distributor's only means

of compliance would be to curtail its existing, non-Large-Load native customers.12

         SMECO asked the Commission to direct PJM to clarify: (1) whether an Electric

Distributor's obligation under an IRAS Action is capped by the New Large Load MW actually

energized and taking service at the time of the Action; (2) if not, what safeguard prevents an

Electric Distributor from being directed to reduce more load than its energized New Large Load

represents; and (3) whether PJM will adjust or suspend an assigned IRAS obligation when the

underlying New Large Load's in-service date is delayed.13

 The PJM Answer does not respond to any of these questions. Instead, it restates the zone-level

design that gives rise to SMECO's concern:

     •   PJM "will be issuing broad load reduction directives to Electric Distributors."14
     •   Electric Distributors "will retain full discretion" as to how PJM's MW reduction
         instructions "will ultimately be carried out just as they do today."15
     •   PJM's directives "will be informed by the degree to which load in a certain zone/area's
         IRAS responsibility has been reduced through MW of BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP
         MW."16
These statements do not account for New Large Load that is not yet energized or is still ramping.

Discretion over which retail customers to curtail is of no help when the load that created the

obligation is not consuming power. PJM identifies offsets for BYONC and Allocated RBP UCAP

MW, but no corresponding adjustment for delayed in-service dates.

         This gap matters because it runs counter to IRAS's stated purpose. PJM describes IRAS as

protecting "native loads from the cost and reliability impacts" of New Large Loads that have not

brought capacity.17 Under the design as filed, an IRAS Action could instead fall on native load.

PJM also states that “[i]n particular, the in-service date is a critical piece of information" collected

through the Large Load Registry.18 The data needed to cap an Action at energized New Large Load

MW will therefore be available to PJM.

         SMECO is not alone in this concern. In its answer, the NJBPU observed that SMECO's

Limited Protest "highlight[s] that this is not merely a hypothetical scenario," because an Electric

Distributor's "assigned New Large Loads may not be yet energized, or may have only just begun

a ramp or testing period that is below its expected draw when PJM issues an IRAS Action."19 The

 NJBPU agreed that SMECO had raised, as did Buckeye Power and East Kentucky Power

Cooperative in their pleadings in this docket, that requiring Electric Distributors to curtail other

customers to meet the assigned IRAS MW amount is "clearly not PJM's intent," and asked PJM to

clarify how it will use real-time demand from New Large Loads to inform curtailment directives.20

The NJBPU also supported SMECO’s and Buckeye Power’s request also made for clarification

that Electric Distributors "will not be required to shed more load than what is being used by New

Large Loads in real-time."21

        The Commission should direct PJM to (1) cap an Electric Distributor's obligation under an

IRAS Action at the New Large Load MW actually energized and taking service in its zone/area at

the time of the action, or explain on the record what alternative safeguard prevents curtailment of

native load; and (2) adjust or suspend an Electric Distributor's assigned IRAS obligation when an

underlying New Large Load's in-service date is delayed.


B. PJM Did Not Respond to SMECO's Protest of the Billing Indemnification Provision.

        In its Limited Protest, SMECO showed that proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section

X(b)(iii) provides that any default in the payment of IRAS compensation "shall be assessed to the

Electric Distributor," not to PJM or its membership. 22 In restructured states, the defaulting LSE

may have no affiliation, and no commercial or credit relationship, with the Electric Distributor.23

The proposal includes no collateral requirement or PJM-administered mutualization to protect the

Electric Distributor.24

         While the PJM Answer addresses IRAS compensation25, the discussion does not mention

section X(b)(iii), default allocation, or Electric Distributor credit exposure. What the PJM Answer

does say, however, underscores the problem. PJM describes the mechanism as "compensating

LSEs, which are NITS customers."26 PJM further states that the entities to be paid and the loads to

be charged are "determined at the state level."27 If the wholesale compensation flows to LSEs, and

payors and payees are set by state authorities, PJM offers no reason why an Electric Distributor

should guarantee payment by other entities.

        In its Answer, PJM consents to clarifying proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X on

compliance, and asks the Commission to "prescribe the compliance requirement in as much detail

as possible."28 SMECO agrees that compliance is the appropriate vehicle. The Commission should

direct PJM, in that compliance filing, to revise section X(b)(iii) so that an Electric Distributor is

not assessed defaults on IRAS compensation owed by other entities. Alternatives include limiting

an Electric Distributor's payment obligation to amounts it actually collects, or establishing

collateral requirements or PJM-administered credit support for IRAS compensation billing.


C. PJM Did Not Address SMECO's Large Load Registry Concerns, and Its Statements to
Other Parties Leave Them Unresolved.

        SMECO requested that the Commission direct PJM to clarify the scope of an Electric

Distributor's liability for Registry information sourced from LSEs or Large Loads29 The PJM

Answer does not respond to SMECO on any of this point. In response to Old Dominion Electric

Cooperative and East Kentucky Power Cooperative, PJM states that the obligation to provide

 Registry information "is borne by the LSE, not the Electric Distributor directly, although PJM

would welcome information provided by an Electric Distributor."30 SMECO indeed welcomes

that clarification. It does not, however, resolve SMECO's concern, for three reasons:

     •   Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III(b) still provides that an Electric Distributor
         "shall" provide Registry information and coordinate with PJM on its validity. A voluntary
         role described in an answer does not modify mandatory tariff language.
     •   PJM states that Electric Distributors "may provide the information for the Large Load
         Registry on behalf of their relevant LSEs," and that PJM may reach out to Electric
         Distributors to supplement LSE submissions.31 That is precisely the relay role for which
         SMECO sought clarity on exposure under FPA section 222 and 18 C.F.R. § 35.41(b),
         which the IRAS Filing itself invoked.32 PJM does not address that exposure.
     •   PJM acknowledges that the RAA's definition of "Party" is broader than LSEs, and that PJM
         "will continue to evaluate this."33 The identity of the obligated entity therefore remains
         unsettled.
         The Commission should direct PJM to conform proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section

III(b) to PJM's stated position that the LSE bears the Registry reporting obligation, and to clarify

that an Electric Distributor that relays, in good faith, information originating with an LSE or Large

Load is not responsible for the accuracy of that information.


D. The Commission Can Resolve These Issues Through Prescriptive Compliance Directives.

         PJM asks that, to the extent the Commission rejects any element of its filing, the

Commission "either direct prescriptive changes to be implemented on compliance or provide

guidance" to PJM and stakeholders.34 SMECO's requests are limited and can be addressed in that

manner.

 IV. Conclusion

       For the foregoing reasons, SMECO respectfully requests that the Commission (1) grant

SMECO leave to file this Limited Answer and accept it into the record; and (2) in acting on the

IRAS Filing, direct PJM to make the clarifications and revisions described above and in SMECO’s

initial Limited Protest.

Respectfully submitted,
